name: Lob Defense / Switching
summary: When a lob goes over your head, the pair has to decide in about a second who chases it and whether you swap sides. Getting the ball back is only half of it — the other half is that the two of you end up in the right places afterwards, which almost always means switching.
whenToUse: A lob has gone over one of you and neither can reach it without turning.
The ball is over the head of the partner who is furthest from it.
You are the one with a clear run at it and your partner is not.
Any lob at all, really — the decision has to be automatic, not negotiated.
howTo: Whoever can reach it calls it immediately: one word, loud, before moving.
Turn and run rather than backpedalling — you cannot get there facing forward.
If you can get under it, hit an overhead; if you can only reach it, lob it back high and deep.
The partner who did not chase slides across to cover the side that was vacated.
Stay switched. Sorting the sides out later is far cheaper than doing it mid-rally.
Recover forward together once the ball is neutral again.
commonMistakes: Both partners turning for it, which leaves nobody anywhere.
Backpedalling, which is slow and is how people land on their wrists.
Chasing it down brilliantly and then both standing on the same side of the court.
Trying to switch back immediately, in the middle of the point.
Not calling it, on the assumption your partner can see what you are doing.

drills.name: Call it and go
drills.description: Two of you at the kitchen line, a feeder lobbing to random sides. Whoever chases must call it before moving and the other must switch. Any rally where nobody called is a loss regardless of what happened to the ball.

drills.name: Turn, do not backpedal
drills.description: No partner needed. A feeder lobs and you practise turning and running to the ball rather than shuffling backwards. Have somebody watch and stop you the moment your feet go backwards.
